Impeachment of Andrew Johnson. The Senate trial of the seventeenth President in eighteen-sixty-eight for allegedly violating the Reconstruction Acts and the Tenure of Office Act. Driven by Radical Republicans led by Thaddeus Stevens who sought to remove a president they viewed as obstructing Reconstruction and Black civil rights, the House impeached Johnson on eleven articles. The Senate fell one vote short of the two-thirds majority required for conviction, preserving the presidency but marking the first presidential impeachment and establishing a precedent for using impeachment as a political weapon.

The impeachment began in early eighteen-sixty-eight when Johnson dismissed Secretary of War Edwin Stanton, supposedly violating the Tenure of Office Act requiring Senate approval for cabinet dismissals. The Tenure of Office Act itself was constitutionally dubious and designed specifically to protect radical-aligned cabinet members from presidential removal. Radical Republicans were enraged by Johnson's lenient Reconstruction policies and his opposition to the Fourteenth Amendment, which guaranteed Black civil rights.

Led by Stevens, the House voted one hundred twenty-six to forty-seven to impeach, generating eleven articles of charges focused on the Stanton dismissal and obstruction of Reconstruction. The Senate trial lasted over two months. Conviction required thirty-six votes out of fifty-four senators, a two-thirds supermajority. On the pivotal vote, the Senate fell exactly one vote short: thirty-five for conviction, nineteen for acquittal. Edmund Ross and others broke party ranks to vote for acquittal.

Johnson remained in office but was politically crippled. He never won nomination for a full presidential term and left office discredited, having demonstrated that impeachment could become a tool of political warfare.
